correctness.rationale: The neighborhood complex splits by the two bipartition classes. On the point side, block simplices have pairwise intersections of at most one vertex; on the block side, point-star simplices intersect in exactly one block. A proved relative-collapse lemma collapses each simplex, independently of the others, to a spanning tree retaining all vertices. The two collapsed graphs have respectively v vertices with b(k-1) edges and b vertices with v(r-1) edges; both are connected, and bk=vr makes both cycle ranks equal to mu=vr-v-b+1. The standalone verifier reconstructs four concrete Steiner designs and replays the elementary collapses without extrapolating from them.

originality.rationale: The checked primary neighborhood-complex literature supplies the general framework and a low-degree classification but not the stated all-Steiner-design collapse or its exact rank formula. Scientific-index searches under design, incidence, linear-hypergraph, projective-plane, neighborhood-complex, and wedge aliases found no statement implying the theorem. The closest same-family indexed result concerns scale-two Vietoris–Rips complexes, which uses a different simplex condition and does not imply the neighborhood-complex statement.
residual_risks: An older or unindexed theorem on simplicial complexes of linear hypergraphs may encode the relative-collapse lemma in more general language and could make the statement a corollary.
The Fano-plane specialization is qualitatively covered by Shukla's maximum-degree-three theorem, although the all-design formula and exact multiplicity are not supplied there.
Scientific-index and web searches cannot establish absolute novelty.

value.rationale: This is an all-parameter structural theorem for a canonical topological graph functor on every nontrivial Steiner 2-design, not an isolated finite census. It identifies the complete simple-homotopy type of both neighborhood-complex components and shows that both remember exactly the cycle rank of the incidence graph. The projective-plane specialization gives the natural closed formula q^3 and applies equally to Desarguesian and non-Desarguesian planes whenever they exist.
